title: Acute limb ischaemia and the saddle embolus
text:
Acute limb ischaemia presents with the six Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia and paralysis; sensory and motor loss mean the limb is threatened within hours. Emboli (mostly from the left atrium in atrial fibrillation or from mural thrombus after infarction) lodge at bifurcations where the vessel narrows: the common femoral bifurcation most often, then the popliteal trifurcation and the aortic bifurcation.
A saddle embolus at the aortic bifurcation makes both legs cold, mottled and paralysed and can be mistaken for spinal cord compression. Embolism is sudden with normal contralateral pulses; thrombosis of an atherosclerotic artery is often less abrupt because of collaterals, with a history of claudication.
Treatment: immediate heparin, then embolectomy with a balloon catheter through the femoral arteries, or bypass or catheter-directed thrombolysis for thrombosis. Reperfusion releases potassium, acid and myoglobin (hyperkalaemia, arrhythmias, acute kidney injury) and swells muscle, so compartment pressures are watched and fasciotomy is often needed.

title: Superficial femoral artery occlusion and the profunda collaterals
text:
The femoral artery is the commonest site of lower limb atherosclerosis, typically occluding in the adductor canal where it passes through the adductor hiatus. The deep femoral (profunda) artery, arising 3 to 4 cm below the inguinal ligament, then keeps the leg alive: its perforating branches anastomose with the genicular arteries around the knee to refill the popliteal artery. Such patients have calf claudication with a palpable femoral but absent popliteal and foot pulses, and rarely lose the limb unless the profunda is also diseased.
Profundaplasty (endarterectomy and patch angioplasty of the profunda origin) can relieve rest pain when femoropopliteal bypass is not possible. Femoral punctures made too low risk the profunda or a pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula between it and the femoral vein; punctures above the inguinal ligament risk uncompressible retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

title: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome
text:
An abnormal relationship between the popliteal artery and the medial head of gastrocnemius (most often the artery looping medial to the muscle's origin) or a fibrous band compresses the artery with each contraction. It causes calf and foot claudication in young athletes and military recruits, who have no risk factors for atherosclerosis. Foot pulses are normal at rest but disappear on active plantarflexion or passive dorsiflexion of the ankle. It is bilateral in about a quarter of cases.
Untreated, repeated compression damages the wall, causing stenosis, post-stenotic aneurysm, thrombosis and distal embolism. Duplex ultrasound with provocative manoeuvres, then MR angiography, confirm it; treatment is surgical release of the muscle, with bypass if the artery is damaged. Cystic adventitial disease of the popliteal artery is another cause of claudication in young men.

title: Foot pulses and the ankle-brachial pressure index
text:
The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt on the dorsum of the foot lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, over the intermediate cuneiform; it is congenitally absent or replaced by a perforating fibular branch in up to 10% of people. The posterior tibial pulse lies behind the medial malleolus, midway between it and the heel, between the tendons of flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus.
The ankle-brachial pressure index is the highest ankle systolic pressure (dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial, by Doppler) divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure. Normal is about 0.9 to 1.3; below 0.9 indicates peripheral arterial disease, below about 0.5 severe disease with rest pain or tissue loss. An index above 1.3 means calcified, incompressible arteries (diabetes, chronic kidney disease), so toe pressures are used instead. Compression bandaging for venous ulcers is unsafe with a significantly reduced index (below about 0.8). Buerger test: pallor on elevation and dusky rubor on dependency indicate critical ischaemia.

targets: Anterior division of internal iliac artery
title: Internal iliac artery: pelvic haemorrhage and embolisation
text:
The internal iliac artery divides at the greater sciatic notch into a posterior division (iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries) and an anterior division (umbilical, obturator, vesical, uterine, middle rectal, internal pudendal and inferior gluteal arteries).
In unstable pelvic ring fractures most bleeding is venous from the presacral plexus, controlled by a pelvic binder placed over the greater trochanters (not the iliac crests) and pre-peritoneal packing; arterial bleeding, commonly from the superior gluteal artery at the notch, is treated by angioembolisation. In postpartum haemorrhage the uterine arteries or anterior divisions can be embolised or ligated, and rich collaterals preserve fertility.
Covering both internal iliac origins during endovascular aneurysm repair, or bilateral stenosis, causes buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction and, rarely, colonic or spinal ischaemia.

title: May-Thurner (iliac vein compression) syndrome
text:
The right common iliac artery crosses in front of the left common iliac vein and compresses it against the fifth lumbar vertebra. Chronic pulsatile compression causes intimal webs (spurs) in the vein. This explains why deep vein thrombosis is more common in the LEFT leg and why extensive left iliofemoral thrombosis may occur in young women, often triggered by the contraceptive pill, pregnancy or immobility.
Suspect it with left-sided iliofemoral DVT, recurrent DVT, or chronic left leg swelling and venous claudication. CT or MR venography and intravascular ultrasound show the compression. Treatment of acute extensive thrombus may include catheter-directed thrombolysis followed by venous stenting of the compressed segment, which reduces recurrence and post-thrombotic syndrome.

title: Proximal deep vein thrombosis and phlegmasia
text:
Proximal DVT (popliteal vein or above) carries most of the risk of pulmonary embolism. The vessel once called the 'superficial femoral vein' is a DEEP vein; the misleading name has led to untreated thromboses, so it is now simply the femoral vein.
Diagnosis: a Wells score, D-dimer when probability is low, and compression ultrasound, in which a normal vein collapses under the probe and a thrombosed one does not, at the common femoral and popliteal veins. Treatment is anticoagulation (a direct oral anticoagulant or low molecular weight heparin) for at least three months.
Massive iliofemoral thrombosis causes phlegmasia alba dolens (a white, swollen, painful leg) and then phlegmasia cerulea dolens, a blue, massively swollen leg whose venous outflow is so obstructed that arterial inflow stops, leading to venous gangrene and shock; it needs urgent thrombolysis or thrombectomy. Post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic swelling, pain, skin change and ulcers) affects up to half of patients after proximal DVT.

title: Venous, arterial and neuropathic leg ulcers
text:
Perforating veins carry blood from the superficial to the deep system through the deep fascia, their valves preventing reflux. When valves in the perforators or deep veins fail, the calf pump drives blood outward, causing sustained venous hypertension in the skin of the lower leg. The results are pitting oedema, haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema, lipodermatosclerosis (an 'inverted champagne bottle' leg) and atrophie blanche, then shallow, sloughy, relatively painless ulcers in the gaiter area, especially above the medial malleolus.
Arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out and deep, on the toes, heel or pressure points, with cold skin and absent pulses. Neuropathic ulcers in diabetes lie under pressure points such as the metatarsal heads, with thick callus and preserved pulses unless disease coexists. A non-healing ulcer with rolled edges may be a squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer) and should be biopsied.
Venous ulcers heal with multilayer compression once the ankle-brachial index is known to be safe, plus correction of superficial reflux (endovenous ablation).

title: Arteriovenous fistulas for haemodialysis
text:
An arteriovenous fistula is the preferred long-term haemodialysis access. The first choice is a radiocephalic (Brescia-Cimino) fistula at the wrist in the non-dominant arm, then a brachiocephalic fistula at the elbow, then a brachiobasilic fistula in which the deep basilic vein is transposed to a superficial position. Patients with progressive kidney disease should have the veins of the non-dominant arm preserved: no cannulas, venepuncture or PICC lines there.
A fistula needs about 6 weeks to mature; a useful guide is the 'rule of 6s' (flow over 600 mL/min, diameter over 6 mm, less than 6 mm deep). A good fistula has a continuous thrill and bruit; loss of the thrill suggests thrombosis. Complications include steal syndrome (hand ischaemia distal to the fistula, worse with brachial fistulas and in diabetics), venous stenosis, aneurysmal dilatation, infection, haemorrhage and high-output heart failure.

title: Palmar arches and hand lacerations
text:
The superficial palmar arch, mainly from the ulnar artery, lies just deep to the palmar aponeurosis at about the level of the distal border of the fully abducted thumb (roughly Kaplan's cardinal line); the common palmar digital arteries and nerves leave it towards the fingers. The deep palmar arch, mainly from the radial artery, lies about 1 cm more proximally on the bases of the metacarpals, with the deep branch of the ulnar nerve in its concavity.
Palm lacerations can bleed briskly from both ends of a divided arch. Bleeding is controlled by direct pressure and elevation (with a tourniquet in theatre), never by blind clamping, which crushes the digital nerves that lie next to the arteries. Before exploration, sensation and capillary refill of every finger are documented. The two arches and the Allen test explain why radial artery harvest or occlusion is usually tolerated.

title: Splenic vein thrombosis and sinistral portal hypertension
text:
The splenic vein runs along the posterior surface of the pancreas to join the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck, forming the portal vein. Pancreatitis (acute or chronic), pseudocysts and pancreatic cancer can thrombose it.
The spleen then drains through the short gastric and gastro-epiploic veins to the stomach, producing isolated gastric fundal varices and splenomegaly with NORMAL liver function and normal portal pressure: 'left-sided' (sinistral) portal hypertension. Upper gastrointestinal bleeding from gastric varices in a patient with pancreatic disease and no cirrhosis should suggest it. Splenectomy (or splenic artery embolisation) is curative because it removes the inflow. It is one of the few surgically curable forms of portal hypertension.

title: Marginal artery and colonic ischaemia after aortic surgery
text:
The marginal artery (of Drummond) runs along the mesenteric border of the colon, linking branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries. When the inferior mesenteric artery is ligated at an abdominal aortic aneurysm repair or during anterior resection, the left colon survives on this arcade from the middle colic artery and, for the rectum, on the middle and inferior rectal arteries from the internal iliacs.
The marginal artery is weak or discontinuous near the splenic flexure (Griffiths point) in some people, so ischaemic colitis follows aortic surgery in a few per cent, usually of the sigmoid colon: bloody diarrhoea in the first days after operation should prompt urgent sigmoidoscopy, since transmural infarction is often fatal. An enlarged 'meandering mesenteric artery' (arc of Riolan) on angiography is a sign of significant SMA or IMA occlusion. In anterior resection a 'high tie' at the IMA origin gives a better node yield, and the marginal artery then decides the viability of the descending colon used for the anastomosis.

title: Colon cancer resections follow the arteries and their nodes
text:
Colonic lymph passes from epicolic and paracolic nodes to intermediate nodes along the named arteries and then to the central nodes at the origins of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries. Cancer resections therefore remove the segment of colon supplied by the named artery with its mesentery, dividing the artery at its origin (central vascular ligation, complete mesocolic excision). At least 12 nodes are examined for staging.
Caecal and ascending colon cancers: right hemicolectomy, dividing the ileocolic, right colic (absent in many people) and right branch of the middle colic arteries. Hepatic flexure and transverse colon: extended right hemicolectomy with the middle colic artery. Splenic flexure and descending colon: left hemicolectomy (left colic artery). Sigmoid: sigmoid colectomy or high anterior resection with the IMA or sigmoid arteries.
Nodal involvement (stage III) is the main indication for adjuvant chemotherapy. Venous bleeding from the gastrocolic trunk of Henle is a recognised hazard when dissecting the middle colic vessels.

title: Gastric cancer lymph node stations and the left gastric artery
text:
Gastric lymph follows the arteries along the lesser and greater curvatures (left and right gastric, gastro-omental and short gastric vessels) to nodes around the pylorus, then to nodes along the left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries and finally the coeliac nodes. A D2 gastrectomy, standard for curable cancers, removes the perigastric nodes plus those along the left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries and around the coeliac trunk; at least 15 nodes are needed for staging. Spread beyond, to para-aortic nodes, the left supraclavicular node (Virchow), umbilicus or ovaries, indicates incurable disease.
The left gastric artery, the largest branch to the stomach, runs along the lesser curvature; lesser curve ulcers erode it, causing major haematemesis, and it is a common target for angiographic embolisation. Its companion, the left gastric (coronary) vein, drains into the portal vein and forms the portal side of the oesophageal varices.

title: Oesophageal cancer spread and oesophagectomy
text:
The oesophagus has a dense longitudinal submucosal lymphatic plexus, so tumour cells travel long distances within the wall (skip lesions) and nodes far from the primary may be involved. Broadly, the upper third drains to deep cervical and paratracheal nodes, the middle third to posterior mediastinal and tracheobronchial nodes, and the lower third to the left gastric and coeliac nodes. The absence of a serosa allows early local invasion of the trachea, aorta and recurrent laryngeal nerves.
Squamous cell carcinoma (smoking, alcohol, hot drinks, achalasia) is commonest in the upper and middle thirds; adenocarcinoma (reflux, Barrett oesophagus, obesity, white men) in the lower third and gastro-oesophageal junction. Treatment of resectable disease is neoadjuvant chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy, then oesophagectomy, commonly the Ivor Lewis operation (abdominal and right thoracic approach with the stomach pulled up as a conduit). Complications include anastomotic leak, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, chylothorax from thoracic duct injury and pneumonia.

title: Lung cancer nodal staging
text:
Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes are N1. Ipsilateral mediastinal nodes, including the paratracheal (stations 2 and 4), subaortic in the aortopulmonary window (station 5), para-aortic (6) and subcarinal (7, the inferior tracheobronchial nodes), are N2. Contralateral mediastinal or hilar nodes and any scalene or supraclavicular node are N3, which generally makes the tumour unresectable.
Left upper lobe tumours spread to the aortopulmonary window, where nodes compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking under the arch, so hoarseness indicates advanced disease. Enlarged subcarinal nodes widen the carinal angle.
Staging combines CT and PET-CT with tissue sampling: endobronchial ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) reaches paratracheal, subcarinal and hilar stations; cervical mediastinoscopy reaches paratracheal and subcarinal nodes but not stations 5 and 6, which need anterior mediastinotomy (Chamberlain procedure) or thoracoscopy. Oesophageal ultrasound can sample the lower posterior mediastinum.

title: Neck node levels and neck dissection
text:
Neck nodes are grouped into levels that predict the primary tumour. Level Ia (submental): lower lip, floor of mouth, tip of tongue. Level Ib (submandibular): oral cavity, anterior nasal cavity, face. Level II (upper jugular, including the jugulodigastric node below the angle of the mandible): oropharynx, tonsil, tongue base, supraglottic larynx; a cystic level II mass in a young adult is HPV-positive oropharyngeal carcinoma until proven otherwise (not a branchial cyst). Level III (mid jugular): larynx and hypopharynx. Level IV (lower jugular): hypopharynx, thyroid, cervical oesophagus. Level V (posterior triangle): nasopharynx, scalp, skin. Level VI (central): thyroid, subglottis.
A radical neck dissection removes levels I to V with the internal jugular vein, sternocleidomastoid and accessory nerve; modified radical dissections preserve one or more of these, and selective dissections clear only the levels at risk. Sacrifice of the accessory nerve causes shoulder drop and pain; bilateral internal jugular ligation risks facial oedema and raised intracranial pressure, so it is avoided or staged.

title: Occipital, mastoid and pre-auricular nodes
text:
Occipital and mastoid (retroauricular) nodes drain the back of the scalp and the auricle. They enlarge in scalp infections, head lice and seborrhoeic dermatitis, and characteristically in rubella, where tender suboccipital and postauricular nodes precede the rash. Painless enlargement with systemic symptoms suggests lymphoma, and in adults skin cancers of the scalp.
Pre-auricular and parotid nodes drain the forehead, temple, lateral eyelids, conjunctiva, anterior auricle and external ear canal. A tender pre-auricular node with a red eye suggests adenoviral or chlamydial conjunctivitis (or Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome in cat-scratch disease). Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma of the scalp, ear and temple metastasise to the parotid nodes, which lie within the gland along the facial nerve, so their treatment is superficial parotidectomy with neck dissection.

title: Retropharyngeal nodes and retropharyngeal abscess
text:
Retropharyngeal nodes lie between the pharyngeal constrictors (buccopharyngeal fascia) and the prevertebral fascia, draining the nasopharynx, adenoids, posterior nasal cavity, middle ear and paranasal sinuses. They are prominent in young children and regress by about five years of age.
Suppuration after an upper respiratory infection produces a retropharyngeal abscess, mostly under five years: fever, neck pain with reluctance to extend the neck, torticollis, drooling, muffled voice and sometimes stridor. A lateral neck radiograph shows widened prevertebral soft tissue (more than about 7 mm at C2), and contrast CT defines it. In adults it follows pharyngeal trauma (fish bone, instrumentation) or tuberculosis of the spine (a cold abscess). Infection can track down the danger space behind it into the posterior mediastinum (mediastinitis). Treatment is airway protection, IV antibiotics and drainage.
The lateral retropharyngeal node (of Rouvière) is a first-echelon node for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

title: Epitrochlear and popliteal lymphadenopathy
text:
Epitrochlear (supratrochlear or cubital) nodes lie above the medial epicondyle beside the basilic vein and drain the ulnar side of the hand and forearm. A palpable node over about 5 mm is abnormal and suggests infection of the little or ring finger or hand, secondary syphilis, HIV, sarcoidosis, or lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
Popliteal nodes in the fat of the popliteal fossa drain the lateral foot and heel along the small saphenous vein and the deep structures of the leg. They enlarge with heel infections and are an in-transit or regional site for melanoma of the heel and lateral foot, which should be examined along with the inguinal nodes.
Both are 'second-line' nodes that are often forgotten: examining them is part of a full lymph node examination in suspected lymphoma.

title: Axillary levels and the internal mammary chain
text:
Axillary nodes are staged relative to pectoralis minor: level I lateral to the muscle (anterior, posterior and lateral groups), level II behind it (central nodes and the interpectoral nodes of Rotter between pectoralis major and minor), and level III medial to it (apical or infraclavicular nodes), which drain into the subclavian trunk and on to the supraclavicular nodes. Spread usually progresses level by level; skip metastases to level III are uncommon. Surgical clearance to level II is standard when an axillary dissection is needed, while sentinel node biopsy (radioisotope and blue dye) is used in clinically node-negative disease.
The internal mammary (parasternal) nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels in the first three to four intercostal spaces and receive lymph from the medial and central breast. They are rarely removed, but their involvement affects radiotherapy fields and prognosis. Rotter node involvement may be missed if only the axilla is examined.

title: Lymphoedema: primary, secondary and filarial
text:
Lymphoedema is protein-rich interstitial fluid from failed lymphatic drainage. Primary forms are congenital (Milroy disease, VEGFR3 mutations), praecox (around puberty, commonest, mainly girls) or tarda (after 35). Secondary lymphoedema is far commoner: after inguinal or axillary node dissection and radiotherapy for cancer, recurrent cellulitis, obesity, chronic venous disease and, worldwide, lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti spread by mosquitoes), which produces elephantiasis of the legs and scrotum and hydroceles.
Early oedema pits; later, fibrosis and fat make it non-pitting, with thickened, warty skin. Stemmer sign, an inability to pinch the skin at the base of the second toe, supports the diagnosis. Management is lifelong: skin care, exercise, manual lymphatic drainage and compression garments (complex decongestive therapy), prompt treatment of cellulitis, and sometimes lymphovenous anastomosis or liposuction. Chronic lymphoedema carries a small risk of lymphangiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome).

title: Whipple operation and resectability of pancreatic cancer
text:
Tumours of the pancreatic head, distal bile duct, ampulla and duodenum are removed by pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple operation): the pancreatic head and uncinate process, duodenum, distal bile duct and gallbladder, the pancreaticoduodenal nodes and sometimes the distal stomach. Reconstruction joins the jejunum to the pancreatic remnant, the bile duct and the stomach or duodenum.
Resectability depends on the vessels behind the pancreatic neck: tumour contact with the superior mesenteric vein or portal vein can be resected and reconstructed, but encasement of more than half the circumference (over 180 degrees) of the superior mesenteric artery or coeliac trunk usually makes it unresectable. Only about 15 to 20% of patients are resectable at presentation.
A replaced right hepatic artery arising from the SMA (about 15% of people) runs behind the pancreatic head and portal vein and must be identified and preserved. The main complications are pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, haemorrhage from the gastroduodenal artery stump and diabetes or exocrine insufficiency.

title: Segmental renal arteries: end arteries and surgical planes
text:
The renal artery divides at the hilum into an anterior branch, which gives four segmental arteries (apical, upper, middle and lower), and a posterior branch that passes behind the renal pelvis to the posterior segment. Segmental arteries are END arteries: occlusion by an embolus, dissection or clamping causes a wedge-shaped infarct of that segment (flank pain, haematuria, raised LDH), and accessory renal arteries (about a quarter of people) supplying a pole cannot be sacrificed without infarction.
The avascular plane between the anterior and posterior territories (Brödel line) lies just behind the lateral convex border, so percutaneous nephrolithotomy tracts and nephrotomies placed through a posterolateral calyx cross relatively few large vessels. Partial nephrectomy for small renal tumours clamps the renal artery or selectively a segmental artery. The posterior segmental artery, crossing behind the pelvis, is at risk during pyeloplasty and endopyelotomy.
